Issued at 120 PM CDT Fri Aug 28 2026

Early this afternoon, a subtle shortwave upper trough was rounding 
the northern periphery of a mid/upper ridge centered over the 
southern Rockies and High Plains. An attendant band of mid-level WAA 
is aiding in the persistence of showers and thunderstorms from 
southwest Manitoba to northeast South Dakota. This activity is still 
forecast to be placed across eastern North Dakota later this 
afternoon and evening. An axis of modest instability (around 500-
1000 J/kg MUCAPE) and sufficient effective shear (around 30-40 knots) 
will continue to support the potential for occasional and isolated 
instances of hail around pennies to quarters in association 
with this elevated convection. Also later this afternoon, 
another subtle shortwave trough will translate eastward across 
southern Montana with a jet max nosing into western South 
Dakota. Despite ample convective inhibition, CAMs are insistent
that convection will develop ahead of this wave given robust 
synoptic ascent. However, this activity will likely struggle 
given the aforementioned CIN, and it's possible only a very
small window exists for the potential of severe weather across 
southern North Dakota during peak diurnal heating late this 
afternoon. Therefore, if a storm can develop during the time of 
minimum CIN and can remain discrete, there is a chance this 
hypothetical storm could produce quarter to golfball size hail 
along with up to 60 mph wind gusts. Most likely though, much of 
the activity today will struggle which is largely the reason SPC
has maintain a marginal (1/5) risk for severe weather for today
and tonight.

Very late tonight into Saturday morning, short range guidance is 
hinting at the potential for a loosely organized backwards 
propagating MCS across southeastern North Dakota. This could 
potentially impact portions of the area from Jamestown to Oakes; 
however much of this activity should remain just east of the area, 
especially given that the LLJ will have veered out and is forecast 
to nose into central Minnesota by daybreak Saturday morning. 
Most of Saturday will end up on the quieter side with afternoon 
highs generally a tick above average in the mid to upper 80s. 
Another subtle shortwave is forecast to round the northern 
periphery of a strong mid/upper ridge (generally centered over 
the central and southern plains), and will be the primary 
catalyst for another round of thunderstorms Saturday evening and
night. Generally speaking, sufficient instability and shear 
should be in place across the southern half of North Dakota to 
support strong to severe storms capable of large hail and 
damaging winds. It's possible a messy storm mode could limit the
large hail threat to an extent; however, DCAPE in the 
neighborhood of 750-1000 J/kg could support some localized 
downbursts with up to 60 mph wind gusts possible. With the loss 
of diurnal heating Saturday eve/night, the intensity of 
thunderstorm activity should gradually decrease. That being 
said, convective inhibition after sunset should be fairly weak, 
and continued broad ascent from a train of perturbations 
embedded in southwesterly flow aloft should continue to support 
sub-severe shower and thunderstorm activity well into the 
overnight hours.

It's a little unclear exactly how activity on Sunday will 
evolve. Mid-range guidance appears fairly confident showers and 
storms will be ongoing through much of the first half of Sunday 
across a large portion of the state well out ahead of a the 
primary trough axis. Given this, it's a bit difficult to pin 
point whether or not the atmosphere will destabilize enough
before the main trough ejects out across the northern plains 
and southern Manitoba. This potential atmospheric 
destabilization will be key to whether or not widespread strong 
to severe storms develop across western and central North Dakota
Sunday afternoon and evening. Given this level of uncertainty, 
SPC elected to go with a marginal (1/5) risk of severe weather 
on Sunday. Details should become clearer over the next couple of
days. Regardless of what occurs on Sunday, a weak cold front is
forecast to sweep across the state Sunday night. This will 
generally lead to temperatures returning to near average for the
beginning of next week. Also, guidance appears to be in good 
agreement that a strong surface low across southern Saskatchewan
will result in a tight pressure gradient across the northern 
half of the state on Monday. Currently, forecast max wind gusts 
Monday afternoon are hovering around 35 to 45 mph. However, 
model soundings indicate deep mixing and uniform flow in the
boundary layer which could allow for locally higher gusts from 
time to time. Additionally, lower RH across the western portions
of the state together with the windy conditions could present 
some fire weather concerns. The parade of upper troughs is 
likely to return by Tuesday and persist through the end of the 
work week next
